The study used a three-bladed rotor with a radius of 13.76 m, divided into 10 equal segments along the radius.
The stochastic lift and drag model was developed based on dynamic measurements of the FX79-W-151A airfoil in a wind tunnel with a turbulence intensity of 4.6%.
The stochastic model is integrated into AeroDyn as an alternative to the static table lookup approach used by the classical BEM model.
The stochastic model parameters, including the drift and diffusion functions, are optimized as functions of the mean angle of attack.
The full field turbulence simulated wind data used as input was generated by the TurbSim program, with a sampling frequency of 20 Hz.
The comparison of the stochastic, dynamic stall, and classical BEM models showed that the stochastic model generates additional dynamic response in terms of local force fluctuations.
The increment probability density functions (PDFs) of the stochastic model results showed slight to pronounced heavier tails compared to a normal distribution, indicating intermittent behavior.
The kurtosis and standard deviations of the increment signals for the stochastic model showed slight to pronounced higher positive values, compared to the classical BEM and dynamic stall models.
The authors state that the stochastic model could lead to improved rotor design optimization by providing more detailed information on the loading conditions.
The current study disregards the tower shadow and other related effects, focusing on the integration of the stochastic lift and drag model into AeroDyn as a primary step.
The authors mention that a future aim is to achieve a complete stochastic rotor model, which could be combined with a wind energy converter (WEC) model.
The study used the IEC von Karman turbulence model with a reference wind speed of 12 m/s and a hub-height turbulence intensity of 15%.
The blade was divided into 10 equal segments, and the results presented are for the 5th element.
The airfoil data file in AeroDyn was replaced with the measured aerodynamic characteristics of the FX79-W-151A airfoil used in the stochastic model development.
The stochastic model is based on a first-order stochastic differential equation, known as the Langevin equation, with parameterized drift and diffusion functions.
